aimShort: Forensic collection of evidence and systematic analysis of a suspect system
board: Pearson BTEC Level 3 National Extended Certificate in IT (AAQ)
assessment: Externally assessed written exam (set + marked by Pearson).

topics.name: Forensics on devices (servers, PCs, mobile): meeting requirements, challenges of live forensics, network forensics, documenting the scene
Systematic forensic analysis of a suspect system
Requirements for accurate records: snapshots, recording findings, recording alterations, visual evidence, relevance/false positives
Assessing findings: evidence of a crime/incident, external/internal compromise indicators
Writing security reports: report structure, preventing recurrence, improving IT policies and protection measures

checklist.name: Forensics on devices (servers, PCs, mobile): meeting requirements, challenges of live forensics, network forensics, documenting the scene
Systematic forensic analysis of a suspect system
Requirements for accurate records: snapshots, recording findings, recording alterations, visual evidence, relevance/false positives
Assessing findings: evidence of a crime/incident, external/internal compromise indicators
Writing security reports: report structure, preventing recurrence, improving IT policies and protection measures

examQuestions.question: State two actions to preserve a seized mobile device for forensic analysis.

points: Retain the current power state/status if possible (1)
Isolate the device from the network/communications (1)
Keep chargers and cables with the device (1)
Use a Faraday bag/cage or disable wireless communication (1)
Document the chain of custody (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain how an investigator should isolate a device that is suspected of communicating so that evidence is preserved.

points: Photograph the screen first to capture what is displayed (1)
Turn off the device or remove the battery/power cable (1)
Use airplane mode or disable wireless communication (1)
Place the device in a Faraday bag/cage to block signals (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain the importance of documenting the chain of custody when collecting forensic evidence.

points: The chain of custody records everyone who handled the evidence, when and what they did (1)
It proves the evidence has not been altered or tampered with (1)
An unbroken chain is required for evidence to be admissible in court (1)
Any gap or inconsistency can make the evidence inadmissible (1)

examQuestions.topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — live forensics
examQuestions.question: Explain two challenges of performing live forensics on a running system.

points: Data is changing in situ — files and memory are being modified while examined (1)
Recovering corrupted data and preventing further corruption is difficult (1)
Capturing data in active memory must be done quickly before it is lost (1)
Remote data must be captured over the network, and temporary files must not be lost (1)

examQuestions.topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — network forensics
examQuestions.question: Explain the steps required before scanning a network for forensic analysis.

points: Agree a network-testing forensics methodology with supervisory and investigatory authorities (1)
Ensure permission is granted to carry out the scan (1)
Ensure the testing protocol will not disrupt a live system (1)
Use passive and active analysis tools appropriately (1)

examQuestions.topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — network forensics
examQuestions.question: Describe the network infrastructure that an investigator would review during network forensics.

points: Firewalls and infrastructure devices — switches, routers, wireless access points (1)
Client or server logs (1)
Malware activity and alerts (1)

examQuestions.topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — documenting the scene
examQuestions.question: Describe how an investigator documents the scene of an incident.

points: Prior planning for a range of scenarios (1)
Securing the scene (1)
Plans, photos and diagrams of the scene (1)
Contemporaneous notes (1)
Witness statements (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain why a hash/checksum is generated for a forensic copy of a system.

points: A hash (checksum) is a digital fingerprint of the data (1)
It proves the forensic copy is an exact match of the original (1)
If the hash changes, it shows the data has been altered (1)
This maintains evidence integrity and admissibility (1)

examQuestions.question: State two requirements for recording forensic findings reliably.

points: No action should change the data on the digital device (1)
Collection must be done by a competent person (1)
A trail/record of all actions taken must be created (1)
Documentation of who is responsible for collection/decisions (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain why an investigator should work with copies/images rather than original data.

points: Working on the original could alter the evidence (1)
Altered data may be inadmissible in court (1)
Using copies preserves the original unchanged (1)
All alterations (intentional or unintentional) must be documented (1)

examQuestions.question: State two forms of visual evidence created during forensic analysis.

points: Photos (1)
Videos (1)
Screenshots (1)
Date-time stamps and metadata (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain how an investigator ensures findings are relevant and not false positives.

points: Define file signatures and search criteria carefully (1)
Know the error rates of the tools and data types used (1)
Feed back false-positive data to improve the detection method (1)
Manually review all positives and further investigate filtered positives (1)

examQuestions.question: State two things an investigator assesses findings for.

points: Evidence of a crime and/or an incident (1)
A regulatory breach (1)
Civil liability or contractual breach (1)
Non-compliance with internal policy (1)
Negligence or mismanagement (1)

examQuestions.question: Describe three indicators that a system has been compromised.

points: Unusual traffic — inbound, outbound or from unusual geographical regions (1)
Unusual login attempts or DNS requests (1)
Increase in file/data reads or requests (1)
Unusual port usage (1)
Suspicious changes to or access to files/data (1)

examQuestions.question: Explain the structure and purpose of a security report written after an incident.

points: A clear structure — title, contents, introduction, headings, numbered/bulleted points, conclusions, footnotes, citations (1)
It analyses the incident to identify errors/omissions in procedures (1)
It identifies errors/delays in detection and remedial actions (1)
It recommends improvements to IT policies and protection measures (physical, software, hardware, processes, training) (1)

examQuestions.question: State two areas of improvement a security report should recommend.

points: Improvements to the content of IT policies (1)
Improvements to physical security measures (1)
Improvements to software or hardware protection (1)
Improvements to processes, procedures and training (1)

mcq.question: When a device is seized for forensic analysis, the first priority is to:

options.label: A
options.text: Preserve the device so evidence is not altered

options.label: B
options.text: Turn it off and forget it

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: Preserving the device prevents data from being changed, which protects the integrity of evidence.
points: A: Preserve the device so evidence is not altered (1)

options.label: A
options.text: Who handled the evidence and when

options.label: B
options.text: The memory size of the device

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: A chain of custody documents the handling history of evidence to maintain its integrity in court.
points: A: Who handled the evidence and when (1)

mcq.question: Forensic investigators work on a copy of the data rather than the original so that:

options.label: A
options.text: The original evidence is not altered

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: Working on a copy preserves the original as unaltered evidence.
points: A: The original evidence is not altered (1)

mcq.question: A hash (or checksum) is generated for a forensic copy to:

options.label: A
options.text: Verify the copy is identical to the original

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: A hash value confirms data integrity — if it matches, the copy is identical to the original.
points: A: Verify the copy is identical to the original (1)

options.label: A
options.text: Evidence that a system may have been breached

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: Indicators of compromise are signs that suggest a system has been accessed or attacked.
points: A: Evidence that a system may have been breached (1)

mcq.question: A security report should finish by recommending:

options.label: A
options.text: How to prevent the incident happening again

mark_scheme.instruction: Award one mark for the correct option.
mark_scheme.explanation: A security report identifies improvements to policies and protection measures to prevent recurrence.
points: A: How to prevent the incident happening again (1)

flashcards.front: How should a seized mobile device be handled?
flashcards.back: Prior planning; retain its current power state; isolate it from the network (airplane mode, disable wireless, Faraday bag); photograph the screen; keep chargers/cables; use appropriate packaging; document the chain of custody; establish legal permissions.

flashcards.topic: D1.1 Forensic collection of evidence — documenting the scene
flashcards.front: What must be done before and during network scanning for forensics?
flashcards.back: Agree a methodology with supervisory/investigatory authorities; obtain permission; ensure the testing protocol won't disrupt the live system; use passive and active analysis tools; review firewalls, switches, routers, WAPs and logs; document the scene (plans, photos, notes, witness statements).

flashcards.front: What are the key requirements for reliable forensic records?
flashcards.back: Retain snapshots (whole disk, files, memory, deleted/temp data) and generate a hash/checksum; take no action that changes data; collect by a competent person; keep a trail of all actions (chain of custody); work on copies, not originals; create visual evidence; avoid false positives.

flashcards.front: What indicators suggest a system has been compromised, and what goes in the report?
flashcards.back: Indicators: unusual traffic (inbound/outbound/regions), unusual logins or DNS requests, increased file reads, unusual port usage, suspicious file changes. Report structure: title, contents, introduction, headings, bullets, conclusions, citations - analysing errors, detection delays, remedial actions and improvements to policies and protection measures.

notes.title: Forensic procedures
passages: [[Chain of custody]] documents who has handled [[evidence]] and when, so it is admissible. Evidence must be collected in [[order of volatility]] — most volatile first (e.g. [[RAM]], running processes, then [[disks]]).
An [[image]] (bit-for-bit copy) is made of the suspect drive rather than working on the [[original]], preserving its [[integrity]].
